implementation_notes: JavaScript inherits through the prototype chain: class User extends LayerObject links User.prototype to LayerObject.prototype, so methods defined once on the base are shared by every instance, super reaches the base implementation, and super(...) must run before this in a derived constructor. With no static types, the layer's declared type is the base class or prototype itself, and membership is checked at runtime with instanceof; older code builds the same link with Object.create or Object.setPrototypeOf, and mixins applied to the prototype (Object.assign, or an extends expression returning a subclass) are the substitute when one base class is not enough. The classic base form remains justified whenever layer members must share identity and state and be recognisable through one prototype.
pitfalls: Methods live on the prototype: mutating LayerObject.prototype at runtime changes every already-loaded layer object, and swapping a prototype breaks instanceof for existing instances.
Derived-class field initializers run after super(), so a base constructor that calls a method the subclass overrides observes a partially initialised object.

There is no declaration separate from implementation: anything of the right shape is accepted by duck typing, so the layer's declared type is only as strong as the instanceof checks and documentation around it.
